title: COMPASS: Temporally Consistent Topological Passing Decisions for Socially Aware Robot Navigation
content: Service robots in crowded pedestrian environments re-decide at every control cycle which side to pass a person on; when this re-decision is greedy, the passing direction can oscillate across cycles in ambiguous configurations, or the robot can freeze. Topology-aware planners bias selection toward the previously chosen class through soft costs, selection hysteresis, or consistency weights; opinion-dynamics methods make the passing side an explicit, stateful decision with deadlock-breaking guarantees; and minimumdwell or fixed-rate selectors bound the switching rate by construction. We introduce COMPASS (COMmitment-based PASSing for Social navigation), a decision-layer planner whose commitment rule is a leaky evidence accumulator — a rectified, leaky variant of Page’s one-sided CUSUM statistic with a progress-dependent threshold — under a lexicographic safety override of the standard priorityarbitration kind. Passing classes are bound to person track IDs, a design contract that the current implementation only partly realizes. We state five properties (P1–P5); they apply standard arguments and are not new mathematics. The load-bearing one, P2, is a deterministic, pathwise lower bound on the number of control cycles between discretionary switches that follows from the accumulator rather than from a fixed dwell timer; at the default knobs its worst case is 3 cycles (0.15 s) for the fixed dt = 0.05 s of the offline harness (for measured intervals, as in the Nav2 adapter, only an accumulated-time form is claimed). P2 is paired with a conditional response-time bound, and P1 refines it to an exponentially small per-cycle switching probability under a bounded-range, i.i.d., zero-mean (ambiguous) challenger-advantage hypothesis. In an offline harness that drives the actual decision core (5 scenarios × 50 seeds), an immediate-argmin comparator produces about 98 decision changes per encounter under ambiguous ties, whereas COMPASS produces at most one decision change in each tested encounter, as does a 0.6 s persistence (dwell) timer in that scenario; the two rules differ under transient, reversing and intermittent advantage. In a historical decision-core-only measurement, latency at K = 3 (8 classes) is p99 58.6 μs and max 651.3 μs (the max is about 1.30% of the 50 ms budget at 20 Hz). All comparators are internal and self-implemented. Post hoc experiments added in v2 after review (same offline harness) add selectors in the spirit of a previous-class consistency weight and of dwell-plus-relative-improvement selection, all tuned by one procedure. At native noise a tuned consistency weight matches or beats default COMPASS on switch count and the observer statistic; at the highest tested noise levels it produces switches per tie encounter where COMPASS produces none, but its tuned bonus sits at the edge of the pre-declared tuning grid, so this degradation may be overstated. Default COMPASS never reaches the scripted final side of the mid-reversal scenario (0 of 50 runs). Progress hardening is the only tested mechanism that holds a nearly complete maneuver against a late scripted burst of 30 cycles or longer. Closed-loop evaluation, comparison with the published planners and opinion-dynamics passing, and user studies are not performed; they are specified as a planned-evaluation protocol. Code: https://github.com/kjungmo/compass.
